claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists on the Pulumi blog at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
The Pulumi blog post at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from AWS CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied SST's infrastructure to AWS (CDK is AWS-only).
Debugging with AWS CDK was frustrating for SST because of CloudFormation templates.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience than AWS CDK (faster deployments).

The in-article table-of-contents links point to anchors on the post's aliased URL /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ (#the-beginnings-of-sst, #cdk-and-cloudformation-limitations, etc.), which must resolve to the matching headings.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
The SST team concluded that limitations of CDK and AWS CloudFormation were holding them back from empowering application developers.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy the resources.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process.
The CDK/CloudFormation approach leads to difficulty debugging, lack of visibility into the deployment process, and challenges extending or customizing the deployment workflow.
The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation exists and describes AWS CloudFormation.
The SST team expanded its focus beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and found the AWS-centric nature of CDK and CloudFormation a limitation.
The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/#what-is-aws-cdk exists and describes the AWS-centric nature of CDK.
AWS CDK supports only AWS (no multi-cloud support), whereas Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
Debugging with AWS CDK is hard due to CloudFormation, whereas Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as programming languages.
Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower than Pulumi's because of CloudFormation; Pulumi executes deployments directly and faster.
With AWS CDK it is hard to trace errors, whereas Pulumi provides a clear deployment state.
AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, whereas Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, whereas Pulumi offers cross-cloud secret support.
Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; it treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment.
Pulumi is a modern IaC platform that takes a fundamentally different approach to infrastructure management than CDK/CloudFormation.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that is running during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and ability to extend or customize it.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach lets SST's team easily work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
The Pulumi model of "your code is the deployment" aligns more closely with application developers' existing mental models than CDK/CloudFormation.
SST had built higher-level components and abstractions on top of CDK and had to re-implement them for Pulumi.
The SST team aimed for the Pulumi-based version of SST to match the functionality of the CDK-based version and improve on it.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights (linked product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Because Pulumi infrastructure code is the deployment code, SST developers could easily trace issues back to the source and understand what was happening during deployment.
With CDK/CloudFormation, the intermediary format (CloudFormation templates) often obscures the underlying logic and makes problems harder to diagnose and resolve.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
The SST team used Pulumi's extensibility features to integrate with a wide range of cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.
With Pulumi, the SST team was able to easily add support for new providers, enabling users to deploy infrastructure across diverse environments.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure (across multiple cloud providers and on-premises) through a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools.
SST users can write their infrastructure logic in the same programming languages they use for their application code.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks and expanded provider support for cloud and on-premises providers built on Pulumi.

Pulumi Cloud Deployments (linked docs page /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) provides advanced deployment workflows, and SST can use them to deliver faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control over deployment.
Pulumi Insights provides better visibility into the deployment process and monitoring/observability capabilities.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering and DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
The Pulumi signup page is at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications.
In SST's Ion engine, constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3 (temporal claim; SST v3 may already have been released, given the post was updated 2025-03-05).
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST potentially has supplemental income streams such as enterprise services and consulting.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK (and CloudFormation) with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install, no Pulumi account, and no Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3's `sst deploy` uses no CDK and no CloudFormation.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
SST is not the only project that builds on the Pulumi engine (Nitric and Defang make the same choice).
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can build and deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

With SST you define an app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites, etc.), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3's architecture) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.
The SST team has repeatedly described SST's architecture as built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page "What is SST" says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Independent developers who have compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture (SST built on the Pulumi engine).

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside the Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

`platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The `anomalyco/sst` GitHub repository was formerly named `sst/sst`.
`sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and SST itself resolves SST's own components.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
In SST, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls.
In SST, Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs, while SST owns the CLI, component model, and local dev loop.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing their own.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The same Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
By embedding Pulumi, SST gets a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang's Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers: SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket and SST does not require a Pulumi account.
Most SST users never write any Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.

Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, users can define raw Pulumi resources directly inside an SST app, for resources without a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week; 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per npm's download API.
SST's own team page credits the same team that is behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger following (GitHub stars) than SST itself, as observed in September 2026.
SST is still being shipped and maintained; the team's public attention broadening to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode.
Anyone who runs SST is already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; Pulumi policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally; Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used with the same Pulumi engine that SST already runs on, without leaving that engine.

SST's components are defined using Terraform providers that are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
You do not need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.

SST is a strong fit for teams that want an opinionated, full-stack application framework; SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across multiple applications on its own.
